passage: At the family's ancestor-remembrance meal in Kuala Lumpur, Wanjiru stood with her husband's relatives before a small table of photographs, food and lit incense. She had been raised in a different tradition and did not share the belief that the dead would come to eat. Xin, the eldest aunt, handed her three sticks of incense. Wanjiru took them, bowed her head as the others did and stayed silent, neither pretending nor pulling away. Xin's hands trembled as she set out her late husband's favourite dish. Wanjiru noticed the aunt's lips moving, telling him something quietly. Across the room a teenage cousin studied his phone. Afterwards Xin squeezed Wanjiru's arm without a word.

qa.a: Xin handed Wanjiru three sticks of incense.

qa.a: Wanjiru probably felt respectful and a little outside the belief, wanting to take part honestly without pretending.

qa.q: What choice did Wanjiru make that let her join honestly?
qa.a: Wanjiru took the incense, bowed her head as the others did and stayed silent, neither pretending to believe nor pulling away.

qa.q: What might the ritual have meant for Xin as her hands trembled?
qa.a: Xin was probably feeling love and loss for her late husband, and the ritual gave her a way to tell him something quietly.

passage: The whole family filled the small hall at the community centre for the new baby's blessing. Grandpa Francis, eighty and leaning on a stick, insisted on leading the prayer himself, the baby held in his arms. Kiran, in the second row, wasn't a believer and felt awkward, but stood with head bowed. Around Kiran most of the aunts closed their eyes; two uncles checked their watches; a young cousin whispered a joke and stopped when nobody laughed. When Francis said the baby's name, his voice cracked, and Kiran looked up to see him blinking hard and smiling at the tiny face. Afterwards Kiran didn't pretend to have prayed. “Thank you for doing that, Grandpa,” Kiran said. Francis nodded and handed Kiran a piece of cake.

qa.q: Where was the baby's blessing held?
qa.a: It was held in the small hall at the community centre.

qa.q: What was Kiran feeling while standing with head bowed?
qa.a: Kiran felt awkward, since Kiran was not a believer, but still wanted to be respectful.

qa.q: What choice did Kiran make at the end, and why does it show honesty?
qa.a: Kiran said, “Thank you for doing that,” without pretending to have prayed, so the thanks were honest and respectful.

qa.q: What might the blessing have meant to Francis when his voice cracked at the baby's name?
qa.a: Francis was probably moved and proud to bless a new member of the family, and leading the prayer himself seemed to matter deeply to him.

grounding: An adult who does not share the family's belief joins a family blessing, sees how much it means to a grandparent and stays respectful and honest.

passage:
Dear Nandini,
You asked how Nani's Milad went. I went. You know I stopped praying years ago, and I almost made an excuse. But I sat in the corner with the women while the naats were recited, and I watched Nani. Her lips moved with every line. Her hands shook when she raised them. My aunt said Nani had waited all year for this, since Nana died.
I didn't pretend to pray. I also didn't roll my eyes like I used to at sixteen. I passed the rose water, served the sheer khurma and held Nani's elbow when she stood. At the end she squeezed my hand and said, 'You came.' That was the whole point, I think.
Love,
Hafsa

qa.q: What did Hafsa serve at the Milad?
qa.a: The sheer khurma; Hafsa also passed the rose water.

qa.q: What was Hafsa feeling while watching Nani's lips move?
qa.a: Hafsa felt moved and tender, seeing how much the ritual meant to Nani, even without sharing the belief.

qa.q: How did Hafsa take part without pretending?
qa.a: By not faking prayer or mocking it, and instead helping: serving, passing rose water and supporting Nani's elbow.

qa.q: What did Hafsa's presence mean to Nani?
qa.a: Nani had waited all year for the Milad since Nana died, so 'You came' shows she felt comforted and honoured.

grounding: An adult attends a grandmother's religious gathering without sharing the belief, sees what it means to her and takes part respectfully.

passage: Deepika, fair question for your show. How do non-believers handle family rituals? Okay, this is Harsha. Last month my parents did a griha pravesh for their new flat. I'm not religious, and my cousins know it. Some of them expected me to sulk in a corner. I didn't sit at the fire and chant, because that would have felt like lying. But I watched my father's face when the priest tied the thread on his wrist. He'd worked thirty-five years for that flat. His eyes were wet. So I carried the kalash, handed out the prasad and stood behind him the whole time. My aunt teased me, 'Atheist carrying the kalash!' I said, 'I'm carrying it for Papa.' He heard. He didn't say anything, just patted my arm.

qa.q: What did the priest tie on the father's wrist?
qa.a: The thread.

qa.q: What did Harsha feel watching the father's face?
qa.a: Harsha felt moved and protective, seeing his wet eyes after thirty-five years of work for the flat.

qa.q: How did Harsha show respect without pretending?
qa.a: By not chanting at the fire, which felt like lying, but carrying the kalash, handing out prasad and standing behind Papa.

qa.q: What might Harsha's father have felt when he heard 'I'm carrying it for Papa'?
qa.a: Likely touched and proud, which is why he patted Harsha's arm without words.

grounding: An adult attends a family ritual without belief, sees what it means to a parent and takes part honestly and respectfully.

passage: I'm Ankita, and I'll just describe what I saw, because I'm still not sure what I felt. Dadi's Satyanarayan katha was in the living room, the sofa pushed back, everyone on the floor. I don't believe in it; my family knows. My brother Hemant, who does, sat right next to the pandit. Dadi's hands trembled as she poured the milk. She had been ill all winter, and it struck me that she might be thinking this could be her last katha. When the story reached the part where the merchant forgets his promise, Dadi looked straight at me and smiled. I didn't fold my hands like Hemant. I sat beside her, kept the lamp from going out and passed the prasad round the room. Afterwards Hemant said, 'You stayed the whole time.' Dadi said nothing, only kept her hand on my knee.

qa.q: What did Ankita keep from going out?
qa.a: The lamp.

qa.q: What might Ankita have been feeling when Dadi looked over and smiled?
qa.a: Ankita seems moved and uncertain, touched by what the katha meant to Dadi without believing in it.

qa.q: How did Ankita take part with respect and honesty?
qa.a: By not folding hands or pretending, but sitting beside Dadi, tending the lamp and passing the prasad.

qa.q: What does the katha seem to mean to Dadi?
qa.a: After a winter of illness it seems deeply important, perhaps a last chance, and having Ankita beside her clearly comforts her.

grounding: An adult who does not share the belief attends a grandmother's ritual, sees what it means to her and takes part without pretending.

Before. On Tuesday, Mohit told his sister Avni on the phone, "I'll come for Dadaji's barsi puja, but I'm not pretending I believe the priest's part." "Nobody asked you to pretend," she said. "Just come."
During. On Saturday, in the crowded front room, Mohit sat near the edge. He watched Dadi's lips move with the Sanskrit, word for word, her hand steady on the brass lamp. Chachaji, who never cried, wiped his eyes during the offering. When the priest asked the grandsons to pour water, Mohit did it slowly and carefully, without mouthing any mantra.
After. On Monday Dadi phoned him. "You poured it well, beta." "Dadi, I don't really believe all of it." "I know," she said. "You came. That's what I'll remember."

qa.q: What did the priest ask the grandsons to do?
qa.a: The priest asked the grandsons to pour water.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling as he watched Dadi and Chachaji during the puja?
qa.a: He was moved and quietly respectful, seeing how much the ritual meant to them even though he didn't share the belief.

qa.q: How did Mohit take part without pretending or showing contempt?
qa.a: He poured the water slowly and carefully but didn't mouth mantras, and later told Dadi honestly that he didn't believe all of it.

qa.q: How does Dadi see Mohit's presence at the puja?
qa.a: For her, his coming mattered more than his belief; she already knew, and what she will remember is that he came.

grounding: Mohit attends a family ritual he does not fully share, sees what it means to the elders, and takes part with respect and honesty.
